facts.text: Co-director Carl Morano once worked at Troma as its theatrical booker, and joined his co-workers as an extra in Troma's War, the studio's gleefully trashy 1988 war movie.
Late Fee was pitched by its producers Fever Dreams as a horror anthology in the tradition of Creepshow, Tales From the Crypt and The Twilight Zone, with a Halloween video-store wraparound.
Before directing Late Fee, Carl Morano led the Martial Arts Drive-In Movie Review Committee for Joe Bob Briggs' 1990s fan newsletter, We Are The Weird.
Late fees were real money for video stores: in 2000 Blockbuster collected nearly $800 million in them, about 16% of its revenue. By 2009 that had dropped to $134 million.
Co-director Carl Morano distributed Hayao Miyazaki's My Neighbor Totoro in its first U.S. theatrical release, through Troma's 50th St. Films in the early 1990s. Yes, that Troma.
Late Fee co-director John Carchietta also wrote the story for the 2009 horror film The Hills Run Red, which reached DVD from Warner Home Video a month before Late Fee did.
Late Fee had its world premiere in New York City on October 1, 2009, then hit DVD from Media Blasters' Shriek Show label in time for Halloween.
Rick Poli, credited as Devil, is the shop owner who rents the couple his prized horror films. The deal: return them by midnight or pay a late fee.
Stephanie Danielson, who plays The Girl, was crowned Miss Greenbelt in 2002 before turning to acting.
J.D. Brown (The Boy) also played Runt in Wicked Lake (2008), a revenge-of-the-witches horror film produced by Fever Dreams, with Late Fee's directors John Carchietta and Carl Morano as producers.
Morano also directed Class of Nuke 'Em High Part II: Subhumanoid Meltdown (1991) and Part 3 (1994), two Troma sequels about radioactive high schoolers.

Variety's Joe Leydon called Wicked Lake, a Fever Dreams film made by Late Fee's producers, a "laughably inept mix of softcore sexploitation and full-bore torture porn." Dread Central gave it 3.5 of 5.
The film was shot in New Jersey, the Garden State, standing in for one very spooky Halloween night.
Coolest Little Monster writer John Zacherle's 1958 hit Dinner With Drac peaked at No. 6 on Billboard's pop chart. The BBC banned it that year for being too scary for young listeners.
The soundtrack includes Coolest Little Monster, written by John Zacherle and performed by punk band Electric Frankenstein on their album E.F. Conquers the World.
Co-director Carl Morano took 2nd place in the Famous Monsters of Filmland magazine trivia contest at the Famous Monsters Convention in New York City.
Dick Clark found Dinner With Drac, a hit by Coolest Little Monster writer John Zacherle, too gory for American Bandstand. Zacherle cut a tamer version, and both ended up on one single.
Stephanie Danielson (The Girl) later won Best Supporting Actress at the Big House LA Festival for playing Cat Donovan in the film The Runaway.
Blockbuster peaked at about 9,100 stores in 2004. It filed for bankruptcy in 2010, a year after Late Fee's video-store setting was already fading.
Late Fee's distributor Shriek Show was the horror label of Media Blasters, founded in 2001 to remaster obscure horror and exploitation films for DVD.
Georgia Kate Haege, who plays The Woman, later turned up on Madam Secretary and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.
Rotten Tomatoes lists Victor Bonacore as playing Dracula in Late Fee, so the Count himself turns up in this anthology.
Coolest Little Monster writer John Zacherle, TV's "Cool Ghoul," died October 27, 2016, at 98. Late Fee hit DVD on October 27, 2009.
One of the film's stories, Damnation, is also listed on IMDb as its own 2009 short, directed by John Carchietta. Late Fee is an anthology.
Co-director John Carchietta's other 2009 credit, The Hills Run Red, was shot in Sofia, Bulgaria, in June and July 2008, on a reported $4.5 million budget.
Shriek Show, which released Late Fee on DVD, and its Fresh Meat line for new directors were both discontinued by parent company Media Blasters in 2013.
